overview: A single airgram from the American Consulate General at Shanghai reports the controversy caused by the Japanese freighter Seibarei Maru’s arrival at Chinwangtao (modern Qinhuangdao) in July 1948. Drawing on a Shanghai newspaper report, it describes Chinese shipping interests’ fears that renewed Japanese commercial activity would damage inefficient local enterprises, their allegation that the voyage infringed Chinese navigation rights, and their demand that Chinese authorities negotiate with SCAP to prevent similar incidents.

subfiles.title: Airgram from Shanghai on the Seibarei Maru controversy
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese shipping interests’ objections to the Japanese freighter Seibarei Maru’s arrival at Chinwangtao and their appeal for action through SCAP.
subfiles.summary: The airgram states that the Seibarei Maru arrived at Chinwangtao on July 19, arousing concern among Shanghai commercial and industrial interests about a revival of Japanese competition. It reproduces a July 22 newspaper account alleging an infringement of Chinese navigation rights and reporting that the vessel departed without a cargo because no Kailan coal was available. Shanghai shipping representatives nevertheless maintained that the issue remained unresolved and urged Chinese authorities to negotiate with SCAP to prevent further Japanese voyages of this kind. The internal reference to 1943 is evidently an OCR error for 1948.

interest: The airgram offers a concise view of Chinese commercial anxiety over Japan’s postwar economic recovery while the Allied occupation was still in force. Its embedded newspaper report documents how a single Japanese freighter’s movement could be framed simultaneously as an economic threat, a navigation-rights dispute, and a matter requiring negotiation with SCAP. It is useful for studying the reconstruction of East Asian maritime trade, Chinese business nationalism, and Japanese re-entry into regional commerce after 1945.
